blocks.p: Before he went to the address Higuchi had given him, Rei went to the two people Gin's file said could feel Nakashima Yuna.

blocks.cap: The underpass where Kubo plays, his guitar case open
Kubo, the blind busker in the underpass

blocks.p: The underpass smelled of wet concrete and frying oil from the stand at the top of the steps. Water dripped somewhere in the dark between the lamps. Kubo, the blind busker, played there by day with his long grey ponytail tied back and his guitar case open at his feet. He could not see the underpass and did not need to. He heard when it turned. When Rei asked about the woman who carried Fear, Kubo stopped playing.
"I always hear her pass," he said. "Like a draught going by with heels on. She hasn't passed in eleven days. The underpass doesn't know what to do with itself."

blocks.cap: The Suzuran at two in the morning

blocks.p: The Suzuran was a cramped place on a Kita corner pressed up against the worst of the thin spots, with one fridge humming too loudly and fluorescent light that made everyone look a day dead. People said the corner did not photograph. Rei believed it. The Woman at the Back sat where she always sat, in the back seat at the Suzuran at two in the morning, in the same coat she wore in every season, a lacquer pin in her long ash-grey hair. She did not look up when Rei stood by her table.

"I'm not telling fortunes," she said. "I'm telling you what's already on its way. You should listen." She turned her cup a quarter turn. "The one who carries fear. I've felt her coming every night for years, like weather. This week I feel her going. Go up her stairs before she runs out of them."

The address was a danchi in Kita. It was one of the long pale public-housing blocks the post-war city had thrown up by the thousand and then forgotten. A four-storey rectangle of identical doors, going grey at the seams, forty metres on the wrong side of where the membrane ran thin.

It was the second week of Obon. Lanterns were out on the ground-floor balconies, paper boxes of orange light hung so the dead could find their way home. Every single one of them was on the south face of the building. Not one hung on the north stairwell. Rei noticed it the way he would have noticed a held breath. Not as a fact but as a pressure. A whole block of living people had quietly agreed, without ever saying it aloud, that there was a part of their own home they did not go into after dark.
He went into it.

The north stairwell was open to the air, concrete treads switchbacking up the outside of the block behind a waist-high wall. The moment his foot left the landing for the first step, the temperature changed. Not the temperature of the air, which was the same wet August heat as everywhere else in the city. The temperature of Rei. Some inner thermostat dropped all at once, as if he had stepped into water he could not see.

It was not a thought. There was no image, no figure, no sound he could point to and call a haunting. There was only the body's oldest verdict, arriving ahead of any reason for it. Do not go up these stairs.

His heart was pounding before he had decided anything. His knees had an opinion. And the worst of it, the part that told him what he was really standing in, was that the fear was not about anything. It had no object. It was simply present in the concrete, the way damp is present, something the structure held. It was reaching into him and using his own nerves to make itself felt.

Halfway up the first flight, on the half-landing where the stairs turned back on themselves, a woman sat on the bottom step of the next flight. Her back was against the wall and her knees were drawn up, and she was shaking.

She was about forty. Black hair with early grey at the hairline, coming loose from a knot that had once been neat. A good dark blazer lay folded on the step beside her, as if she had taken it off days ago meaning to put it back on. She wore a cardigan buttoned wrong and canvas shoes with the laces gone. She had the particular stillness of someone who had made herself small for a long time and had become frighteningly good at it.
She did not look at Rei. She looked at the step above her own as if it were the edge of a cliff.

"You can feel it," she said. It was not a question. Her voice was thin and even, and keeping it even was costing her. "Most people just feel sick and leave. You came up anyway, and you can feel it, which means somebody sent you, which means it's worse than I thought." Her hands were pressed flat to the concrete on either side of her. "Please don't make me explain who I am while I'm sitting in it. Just sit down where you are. Don't come higher. And tell me whether the two of you in there are lit, because I can't hold and read you at the same time any more."
Her name was Nakashima Yuna. She was the fourth of the Thirteen, and she held Fear.

In ordinary life she ran a security consultancy. She was a director, the kind of woman who had made every decision in a building before she walked into it. Her calendar was public. Her assistant knew more than most practitioners. For twelve years she had been building a map of what the fear domain actually produced. Not all of it was hostile, she said. Some of it was defensive. Some of it was warning systems older than the Accord. The CVD used her taxonomy in its training without ever putting her name on it. She had noticed. She filed nothing and did everything.
Since the night her seat had come open, she had been trying to climb back into it. She had not got past the half-landing of her own domain in eleven days.
She told him this in pieces, in that flat careful voice, never raising it. She had learned that her own feelings were the one thing in this stairwell she absolutely could not afford.

"A holder doesn't fight the register," she said. "You carry it. It runs through you like current through a wire, and the wire doesn't get to have feelings about the current. The wire just has to be a wire. The day I started being afraid of my own seat is the day the seat started leaking."
She tipped her head a fraction toward the flights above. In the dimming light the upper landings were stacked grey rectangles.

"It used to live at the top. In the plant room. I'd go up once a week and sit with it, and it stayed put. Now it comes down to meet me. It's on the third landing tonight. Yesterday it was on the fourth. It's learning that I'm scared. Every time it learns, it comes a step closer. And a fear holder who's running out of stairs is a domain about to come off its hinges."

Rei sat with his back against the cold wall and his own pulse hammering at a threat that did not exist. He understood that this was what the inside of a seat felt like. Not the grand thing Higuchi's ledger made it look like, twelve dignified pillars holding up the world. A woman who could not go upstairs, doing the unglamorous arithmetic of how many landings she had left.

The fear was not hers. She kept saying so, gently, the way a mother corrects a child who has got it backwards. The fear in the concrete was the register. The domain. The thing she had been given to carry, and it was as impersonal as weather. But the fear of the fear was hers. Eleven days of dread that she would not be able to climb, that she would fail, that she would be the seat that fell. That part was hers. It was the crack the register had got its fingers into. And she could not stop producing it, because she was human and the stakes were the wall of the world.

"I can steady anyone," she said. "That's the strange part. Put a practitioner in front of me in a full crisis and I can bring them level in under thirty seconds. I've done it in car parks. I've done it in a hospital lift. I can't do it for me."
"Is there no one who could climb with you?"

"Natsumi would. Okabe Natsumi. She holds Courage, the tenth. Our seats are tied together. Fear is seeing the harm coming. Courage is going forward anyway. We've worked in step for twelve years. The first five were difficult." The ghost of a smile. "I haven't called her. I'm afraid that if I lean my whole weight on her I'll pull her down onto the landing with me. Then there would be two of us sitting here."

"I keep thinking if I were braver I could just walk up," she said, and for the first time the flat voice wavered. One hairline crack, and then she pressed it smooth again. "But that's the trap, isn't it. The braver I try to be, the more I'm thinking about being brave. The more I think about it, the more I'm feeling it. And feeling it is the leak. You can't white-knuckle your way back into a fear seat. The only people who can hold Fear are people who genuinely aren't afraid in the moment. I haven't had a moment like that in eleven days."

She finally looked at him. Her eyes did what the others' eyes had done. They read the two registers, the searching, the keyed thing the chair wanted. But where the others had looked at him with caution, she looked at him the way a drowning person looks at something that floats.
"You came up the stairs feeling it," she said. "And your hands were steady. I watched them. How are your hands steady?"
Rei asked her the question he had learned to ask every weakening holder. By now he had seen the shape twice, and he no longer believed in coincidence.

"Has anyone been kind to you lately? Anyone soft-voiced. Anyone who turned up around the time it started getting worse, and helped, and made you feel a little better, and left you a little more afraid than before?"
Yuna went very still in a new way. It was the stillness of someone fitting together two things she had been keeping carefully apart.

"The man from the residents' association," she said slowly. "He's not... I've never seen him at a meeting. He started coming by about two weeks ago. He brings me tea on the landing. He sits a few steps down, like you. And he's so calm. He's the calmest person I've ever met. He asks me how the seat is doing, and he listens, really listens. And when he leaves I always feel..."
She stopped.
"I always feel worse. I thought it was just the contrast. You feel safe with him, then he goes and you're alone with it again. But that's not it, is it. That's not it at all."
It was not it. Rei had read the ledger. He knew the handwriting of this kind of kindness now.

Someone had been coming to the fourth seat with tea and a soft voice and an open ear. On every visit he drew her fear up to the surface. He let her dwell in it. He named it gently back to her. Then he took his calm away and left the fear standing. Not to torment her. Nothing so crude. To train it. To teach the register in the concrete that its holder was afraid. To walk it down one landing at a time toward the moment the seat slipped its mooring and Fear went vacant, right beside a membrane that was already thin.

It was the same design as the Rage seat in the bathhouse. The same patient cruelty wearing the face of help. Not an attack the holders could fight. A kindness they could not refuse, aimed at thinning the wall of the world from the inside by emptying the chairs that held it up. The thirteenth seat was vacant. Someone wanted company for it on the wall that leaned north.

"He's coming tonight," Yuna said. The flat voice had dropped to a whisper, because understanding was itself a spike of the very thing leaking out of her. "He said he'd come tonight to see how I was doing. He's always so worried about how I'm doing."
She looked up the stairs, to the third landing where the grey was thickest. Then down past Rei to the lower flight, where the orange Obon light from the south face barely reached.

"If he comes and sits and does it again, I won't have a fourth landing left. I'll have the plant room, and then the roof, and then nothing. The seat will come off. You felt what one stairwell's worth of it does to a person walking up. Imagine it with no holder. Imagine it loose over Kita during Obon, with the doors already open for the dead."
She took a breath that shook all the way down.
"So I need to know what you are before he gets here. Because I think you might be the only thing in this building that can stand on the landing between us and not break."
The thing Rei did was not the one the stories would have chosen.

He did not climb to the third landing and face the fear down like a thing with a throat he could cut. There was nothing up there to face. What Yuna needed was smaller and far harder. She needed to climb back into her own seat. She could not do it while she was afraid. And she would be afraid the whole way up.

So Rei went up the stairs ahead of her. One step at a time. He stood on each landing as he reached it, and he took the fear that lived there into his own walled-off chest, where it could not get all the way in. He held it. For the length of one breath, the step she was climbing onto was the one place in the building where the dread was being carried by someone else.
He was not removing it. He could not remove it. He was being afraid in the right place, on purpose, half a second ahead of her, so that she stepped onto ground that had just been held.

It was the worst climb of his life. The fear on the second landing was bad. The third was worse. The dread coming off the plant-room door at the top was a physical weight that bent his neck. The body's whole ancient machinery was screaming about a danger with no shape and no end.

The only thing that let him keep his feet was the exact wound he had spent his life ashamed of. The suppression. The wall. The two registers held down so long they had gone half numb. The fear reached into him and found the connection it wanted already cut. He was useful here precisely because he was broken in this particular way.

Somewhere under the dread, a quiet voice he did not like the sound of was saying, see, the wall is good, the wall is a gift, why would you ever take it down. He climbed anyway. He left that voice on the landing below with the rest of what he was carrying.

Behind him, one step down, Yuna climbed into the air he had just made bearable. She was shaking and she did not stop. She did not need to be unafraid. For the first time in eleven days, she was not afraid alone.

At the top, at the plant-room door, she put her hand flat against the steel where the register was thickest. Rei felt it happen. The current found its wire again. The impersonal weather of Fear poured back through its holder instead of pooling loose in the concrete. The whole stairwell breathed out a cold it had been hoarding.

The dread did not vanish from the building. It was a domain. It was supposed to be there. Fear was one of the true things the world was made of, and someone had to carry it. But it went back up into the plant room where it lived, and it stopped coming down to meet her, because she was in the chair again and the chair did not flinch.

Yuna stood with her palm on the door, in her wrong-buttoned cardigan and her ruined shoes, and she breathed. All the way to the bottom of one breath. The first one in eleven days that did not feed the leak.
"Oh," she said, very softly, to the door. "Oh. There you are. I'm sorry. I'm here. I'm not going anywhere."

Rei's knees gave then. He had not known they were going to. He sat down hard on the top step with the dread still ringing in him like a struck bell, his hands shaking now that they were finally allowed to.
Yuna crouched beside him. She did not ask if he was all right. She put two fingers lightly against the inside of his wrist, the way a nurse takes a pulse, and looked him in the eye.

"Breathe out longer than you breathe in," she said. Her voice had changed. It was the voice she must use in car parks and hospital lifts. Calm, exact, carrying. "Again. Feel the step under you. Name three things you can see."
"The door. Your hand. The lanterns."

Something moved under her fingers and through his arm. It was warm and very precise, like a hand adjusting a dial he had not known he had. His heart slowed. His breath came back into his own control. The ringing faded to a hum.
She took her fingers away. "Twenty seconds," she said, with the ghost of professional pride. "I'm out of practice."
"You could have done that for yourself," Rei said.

"No." She stood and looked at the plant-room door. "That's the thing nobody tells you about the steadiest people. We can't steady ourselves. We were never built to. We were built to need someone on the stairs." She looked down at him. "Twelve years I've been mapping what fear really is. It isn't one thing. Some of it attacks. Some of it defends. Some of it is just a very old alarm, ringing because it's been ringing since before there was a city here. The CVD took my list and put it in their manuals. They never took that part." She almost smiled. "This one's an alarm. It was always an alarm. I forgot."
He arrived while they were still at the top.

Rei heard him before he saw him. The unhurried scuff of careful shoes on concrete. The small domestic clink of a flask against a cup. A man was climbing into a stairwell that should have been terrifying, as calmly as if he were coming up to water the plants.

He was unremarkable in the particular way the dangerous ones are. Middle-aged. Soft-faced. A cardigan of his own, kind eyes, a residents' association lanyard he had no right to. He got two landings up before he noticed that the stairwell was wrong for him tonight. The fear had gone home. The holder was in her chair. And someone was standing at the top who was not afraid, watching him climb.
He stopped. He looked up at the two of them with an expression of such gentle, genuine-seeming concern that for one full second Rei understood exactly how he had got into so many rooms.
"Yuna-san," he said warmly. "You're up so high tonight. I was worried. You shouldn't push yourself."

Rei watched her hear it. The worry. The push-yourself. The soft little weight laid on the fear to draw it back up. And he watched it fail. She was in the seat now, and the seat did not flinch. The disappointment that crossed the man's kind face before he smoothed it away told Rei everything about what he had really come for.

He did not fight. His kind never did. Fighting was for registers, and he was not a register. He was a method. He simply took in that tonight's session was not available, recalculated with the frictionless speed of a man who has many other appointments, and began, unhurried, to go back down.

"I'm glad you have a friend," he said over his shoulder, mild as milk. The worst part was that it sounded as if he meant it. Somewhere in the build of him there was something that did experience this as kindness, even while it emptied the chairs that held the sky up. "Everyone should have someone to be brave for them. It's so much harder alone."

He was telling Rei that he knew what Rei had done and how. And he was filing it, the way the soft-voiced ones filed everything. The fourth seat could be re-held with the help of someone with a wall instead of a heart. The keyed thing that had walked up these stairs tonight was exactly the kind of tool the work could use. Rei had come to save a holder. Without meaning to, he had also shown the other side a new tool. They had been taking notes the whole time he climbed.

When the man was gone, and he went all the way, Rei made sure of it, standing at the rail and watching the soft shoulders cross the lit courtyard and pass out under the Obon lanterns until the dark took him, Yuna came and stood beside Rei at the top of the stairwell she could not climb an hour before.

The orange light from the south face threw long warm rectangles across the courtyard. The paper boxes burned low for the dead finding their way home. And on the north face, for the first time in eleven days, the fear was just weather in a plant room, and a woman was holding it.
"He'll go to the next one," she said quietly. "Whoever's weakest. There's always a weakest."

She was not wrong. Somewhere across the thin ward there was a fifth seat, a ninth, an eleventh. Each one was being visited by someone with a flask and a kind face and endless patience, and Rei could not be on every stairwell. But he had been on this one.
"Thank you for being afraid up here," Yuna said.
It was the strangest thanks he had ever been given, and the truest. She meant, thank you for not making me do it alone.

On the way down, Rei stopped on the half-landing where she had sat for eleven days. On the step, tucked against the wall where Rei had sat, lay a paper cup with a little tea still in it. It was cold. It had been there before Rei arrived. The man had already been up these stairs once tonight, early, and had left his cup where Rei would sit, and gone down again to wait. He had not been surprised to find someone at the top. He had come back to see who it was. Rei put the cup in his pocket and walked out under the lanterns with the back of his neck prickling, and did not look round.
